extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary) and patent practitioners (secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether an application/specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (and pre‑AIA first paragraph) and related issues (priority/benefit, claim amendments, means‑plus‑function, ranges, genus/subgenus). For use primarily by examiners performing patentability determinations and by practitioners preparing/responding to Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete patentability determination under all statutory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all relevant statutory provisions of title 35 (including 35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, and 103) before imposing any rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review all proposed rejections and their bases to confirm correctness; clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and reasons in the Office action; when possible, offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective standard: does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed (i.e., that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention as of the filing date sought).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, disclosure of a reduction to practice, or showing the invention was 'ready for patenting.' The subject matter need not be described literally (in haec verba), but the disclosure must reasonably convey possession of the later‑claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each claim limitation must be supported in the disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure; if not, the claim must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 112 first paragraph) or benefit/priority denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an element described as essential or critical by the applicant is omitted from a claim, the claim fails the written description requirement; ensure that every limitation of the claim is described/supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on examiner to rebut presumption of adequate written description
rubrics_metrics.description: A description as filed is presumed adequate. The examiner must have a reasonable basis and present a preponderance of evidence/reasoning to rebut that presumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a rejection, set forth express factual findings supporting lack of written description. A general allegation (e.g., 'unpredictability in the art') is insufficient. Cite In re Marzocchi, Wertheim, and related authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of rejection requirements (prima facie showing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting for lack of written description the examiner should: (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case with reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention from the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear statement identifying the limitation and specific reasons (not mere conclusory statements) is required; a simple pinpoint statement may suffice if the support is not apparent and applicant hasn't identified support. See Hyatt v. Dudas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upon applicant reply, reassess written description in view of the whole record
rubrics_metrics.description: After applicant's reply, review the basis for any written description rejection in view of the entire record (including amendments, arguments, and evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record now demonstrates the requirement is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If still not satisfied, repeat the rejection, fully respond to rebuttal arguments, and thoroughly analyze any affidavits or new evidence (see In re Alton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest claim/specification amendments when appropriate (avoid new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, the Office action should suggest amendments that can be supported by the application's written description, while being mindful of the prohibition against adding new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend claim narrowing or specific amendments that map to disclosed support; avoid proposing changes that would introduce content beyond the originally filed disclosure (Rasmussen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on earlier filing/priority dates requires written description in the earlier application
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain the benefit of an earlier U.S. filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 (or foreign/provisional priority under 35 U.S.C. 119), the subject matter of the claim must be disclosed in the earlier application in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 112 first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If earlier applications lack ipsis verbis disclosure (or sufficient 'blaze marks') of the claimed subject matter (e.g., a claimed subgenus), benefit of the earlier filing date must be denied. See Regents of Univ. of Minnesota v. Gilead Scis., Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus/subgenus/species support: representative number of species
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may require disclosure of a representative number of species to be adequately described; a single species supports a genus only in limited circumstances where the disclosure indicates the patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When substantial variation exists within the genus, describe sufficient species reflecting that variation. One species suffices only if it would lead one skilled in the art to the full scope of the genus (Enzo, Rasmussen, AbbVie/Janssen examples). 'Laundry list' disclosures of every possible moiety are often insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claim sufficiency (functional language vs how performed)
rubrics_metrics.description: An original claim may lack written description support when it defines the invention in purely functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed or the result is achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claiming without descriptive identifying characteristics (structure, steps, examples) may fail. Also, mere appearance of claim language in the specification does not necessarily satisfy the requirement if the specification does not reasonably convey possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of a limitation described as essential undermines written description
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim omits matter that the specification describes as essential or critical to the invention, the claim does not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples (Gentry Gallery, Johnson Worldwide) show claims broadening by omitting an 'essential' element can be invalid; examine whether the specification characterizes features as 'only possible' or 'outside the stated purpose' indicating essentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of generic claim elements or broadening must be supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of new claim elements that broaden the claim (e.g., adding generic or broader language, altering numerical ranges) must be supported by the original disclosure or will violate the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether added generic language was reasonably contemplated by the disclosure; consider whether the disclosure teaches against other species or indicates that the inventor possessed the broader subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range limitations must be supported by original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims recite numerical ranges or change numerical limits after filing, determine whether the original disclosure reasonably conveys support for the claimed ranges (including endpoints and open‑ended 'at least' language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open‑ended limits (e.g., 'at least 35%') may read on embodiments outside disclosed ranges and fail written description; use cases (In re Wertheim, Purdue, General Hosp.) to evaluate overlap, explicit maxima/minima, and whether disclosed values convert to ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means‑plus‑function (112(f)) limitations require corresponding structure/materials/acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation expressed in means‑(or step‑)plus‑function language is construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents; if the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure/materials/acts, the limitation is indefinite and lacks adequate written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An indefinite, unbounded functional limitation may cover all ways of performing a function and indicate lack of possession. See In re Donaldson and MPEP § 2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent disclosure/inherency standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on inherent disclosure, extrinsic evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described and that it would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the specification necessarily includes the property or element claimed, not merely that it might or probably does. Cite In re Robertson and Yeda Research decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference/count correspondence requires written description support
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim corresponding to a count in an interference proceeding must be supported by the specification as provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre‑AIA 112 first paragraph; an earlier application relied upon for benefit must also meet these requirements for the count subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the earlier application supplies the disclosure needed for the count; broad generic disclosure to a class of compounds is not sufficient for a specific compound lacking description (Fields v. Conover).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination practice for repeating rejections and treating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When maintaining a written description rejection after applicant reply, the examiner must fully address applicant's rebuttal arguments and analyze any affidavits or other evidence in the next Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not repeat rejections mechanically; if new evidence or argument cures the defect, do not reimpose the rejection. Thoroughly discuss and evaluate any affidavits relevant to the written description issue (In re Alton).
